tips.title: CnH2n, two hydrogens fewer
tips.body: An alkene always has **two fewer** hydrogens than the alkane with the same carbons: ethane C₂H₆ against ethene C₂H₄. If you can write the alkane you can write the alkene, and that is what *unsaturated* means in one line.

tips.title: Four bonds at every carbon
tips.body: Before you finish a displayed formula, count the lines at each carbon — a double bond counts as two. Three or five bonds is the most common lost mark in this topic, and counting takes five seconds.

tips.title: Decolourised, not clear
tips.body: Bromine water goes from **orange to colourless** with an alkene. Write *decolourised*; *turns clear* does not score, because orange bromine water is already clear — clear means see-through, not colourless.

tips.title: The conditions are marks too
tips.body: Hydrogen needs **nickel at 150 °C**; steam needs **phosphoric acid, 300 °C, 60–70 atm**; bromine needs **nothing at all**. Questions ask for conditions as often as products, so learn them in pairs with their reagent.

tips.title: Count both sides of an addition
tips.body: Nothing else is formed in an addition reaction, so the atoms on the left must equal the atoms on the right exactly. If your product is missing atoms, you have written a substitution by mistake.

why.matters:
An alkane is a dull molecule: it burns, and not much else. Put one **double bond** in it and you have the starting material for plastics, alcohols, antifreeze and most of the organic chemical industry.

The double bond is a **functional group**, and the useful thing about a functional group is that it behaves the same way whatever is attached to it. Learn what adds across a C=C once and you can predict the reaction of a molecule you have never seen.

examples.title: Why margarine is solid and the oil it came from is not
examples.body:
Vegetable oils are unsaturated: their chains carry **double bonds**, which put kinks in the molecule so the chains cannot pack neatly, and the fat is a liquid at room temperature.

Adding hydrogen across those double bonds straightens them out. The product is saturated, packs closely, and is a solid you can spread. It is one addition reaction — nickel catalyst, 150 °C — and it is the whole difference between a bottle of oil and a tub of margarine.

props.title: Hydrogen adds across the double bond: nickel, 150 °C

visual.alt: Ethene with its double bond becoming ethane with a single bond when hydrogen adds across it, the reaction that turns an unsaturated liquid oil into a saturated solid fat

examples.title: Three things that add across a double bond
examples.body:
Addition is the alkenes' reaction: the double bond **opens**, the two new atoms attach to the two carbons, and there is no second product. Nothing leaves.

Three reagents do it, and the conditions are marked as separately as the products. Hydrogen needs a nickel catalyst and heat. Steam needs phosphoric acid and pressure. Bromine needs nothing at all, which is exactly why bromine water works as a test: a reaction that happens on its own, at room temperature, in a test tube.

visual.alt: A table of the three addition reactions of alkenes: hydrogen with a nickel catalyst at a hundred and fifty degrees giving the alkane, steam with phosphoric acid giving an alcohol, and bromine needing no conditions at all

examples.title: The ethanol that never saw a grape
examples.body:
Ethanol for drinking is fermented from sugar. Ethanol for solvents, sanitiser and fuel is mostly made the other way: **steam added to ethene**, over phosphoric acid at 300 °C and high pressure.

It is the same molecule either way, and the two routes are argued about on entirely different grounds — one uses a crop and a fortnight, the other uses crude oil and a continuous plant. The chemistry here is one line: water across a double bond.

visual.alt: The equation for making ethanol industrially: ethene plus steam gives ethanol, over a phosphoric acid catalyst at three hundred degrees Celsius and sixty to seventy atmospheres

steps.title: What makes an alkene an alkene
steps.body:
An **alkene** is a hydrocarbon with a **carbon–carbon double bond**, written **C=C**. That double bond is the whole topic: it is what alkenes have and alkanes do not, and every reaction here happens there.

The general formula is

$$C_nH_{2n}$$

so ethene is C₂H₄, propene is C₃H₆, butene is C₄H₈ and pentene is C₅H₁₀. These four are the only alkene names you need.

Alkenes are **unsaturated**, which means they contain **two fewer hydrogen atoms** than the alkane with the same number of carbons. Compare them directly:

- ethane C₂H₆ against ethene C₂H₄
- propane C₃H₈ against propene C₃H₆

The two missing hydrogens are exactly what the second bond replaced. A molecule with no double bond is **saturated**: it holds as many hydrogens as it possibly can.

steps.title: A functional group, and why it matters
steps.body:
The C=C is called the **functional group** of the alkenes. A functional group is the part of a molecule where the reactions happen — and the important idea is that **it behaves the same way whatever the rest of the molecule is**.

So you do not learn the reactions of ethene, then the reactions of propene, then butene. You learn the reactions of **C=C**, and they apply to all of them. That is why the spec says it is *the generality of reactions of functional groups that determine the reactions of organic compounds*.

This is what makes organic chemistry learnable. Each family has one functional group:

- alkenes: **C=C**
- alcohols: **–OH**
- carboxylic acids: **–COOH**

Learn what each group does, and you can predict the reaction of a molecule you have never seen.

A family of compounds sharing a functional group and a general formula is a **homologous series**. Its members have similar chemical reactions, and their physical properties — boiling point in particular — change gradually along the series as the molecules get bigger.

steps.title: Burning alkenes
steps.body:
Alkenes are hydrocarbons, so like any hydrocarbon they **react with oxygen in combustion reactions**. Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water:

$$C_2H_4 + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 2H_2O$$

But in air, alkenes **tend to burn with smoky flames**, and that is worth being able to explain rather than just recall.

The reason is **incomplete combustion**. An alkene has a higher proportion of carbon than an alkane with the same number of carbons — C₂H₄ against C₂H₆ — so there is relatively more carbon to burn for the oxygen available. Some carbon is not fully oxidised, and it leaves the flame as **soot**, which is the smoke you see.

Incomplete combustion also produces **carbon monoxide**, a toxic gas, and releases less energy than complete combustion.

So a smoky flame is a *symptom*: it tells you the fuel is not getting enough oxygen for the carbon it contains.

steps.title: Addition reactions: the double bond opens
steps.body:
The reaction alkenes are known for is **addition**. Atoms add **across the carbon–carbon double bond**, and the double bond becomes a **single** bond.

Nothing is lost and nothing else is formed — both added atoms end up in the one product. That is the pattern for every addition reaction, whatever is being added.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Write the molecular formula of butene, and of the alkane with the same number of carbons.
2. What does *unsaturated* mean?
3. Name the functional group of the alkenes.

**Part B.**

4. Draw the displayed formula of propene.
5. Propene reacts with hydrogen. Write the equation and name the product.
6. Propene reacts with bromine. Write the formula of the product.

**Part C.**

7. Explain why bromine water is decolourised by an alkene but not by an alkane, in terms of the bonds present.
8. Ethene and ethane both burn. Explain why ethene tends to burn with the smokier flame.

For question 4, count the hydrogens by giving every carbon exactly four bonds — a carbon with three or five bonds is the commonest lost mark in the topic.

steps.title: Going deeper: drawing structures that score
steps.body:
**Every carbon has exactly four bonds.** Not three, not five. When you draw a displayed formula, count the bonds at each carbon before you put your pen down — a double bond counts as two. This single check catches almost every drawing error.

In a displayed formula you must draw **every bond as a line**, including every C–H bond. Writing CH₃ in the corner of a displayed formula is not a displayed formula, and does not get the mark.

**Where does the double bond go?** For butene, C₄H₈, it could sit between the first and second carbons or between the second and third — these are different molecules with the same formula. The spec does not require you to name them individually, but if a question gives you a structure, read where the double bond is before you react it.

**Addition versus substitution.** This distinction is worth being exact about:

- **Addition** (alkenes): atoms join **across the double bond**, which becomes single. One product, nothing else formed.
- **Substitution** (alkanes): an atom is **swapped** for another, so a second product is always formed as well.

Alkanes cannot do addition, because they have no double bond to open. That is the real reason bromine water distinguishes them.

**Why the bromine water test works.** Bromine water is orange because of dissolved Br₂. An alkene **adds** Br₂ across its double bond, so the Br₂ is used up and the colour goes: **orange to colourless**. An alkane has nothing to add across, so the colour stays. Say *decolourised*, not *turns clear* — clear means see-through, and orange bromine water is already clear.

**A check on any addition product.** Add up the atoms on both sides. In an addition reaction they must match exactly, because nothing else is formed. If your product has fewer atoms than the reactants combined, you have written a substitution by mistake.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- An **alkene** is a hydrocarbon with a **C=C** double bond; general formula **CnH2n**.
- The first four are **ethene, propene, butene, pentene** — C₂H₄, C₃H₆, C₄H₈, C₅H₁₀.
- Alkenes are **unsaturated**: **two fewer hydrogens** than the alkane with the same carbons.
- The **functional group** is C=C, and a functional group reacts the same way whatever the rest of the molecule is.
- Alkenes burn, but tend to give **smoky flames** because of **incomplete combustion** — more carbon per molecule, so soot.
- $C_2H_4 + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 2H_2O$ for complete combustion.
- In an **addition** reaction, atoms add **across the double bond**, which becomes single. One product only.
- **Hydrogen**: nickel catalyst, about 150 °C → an **alkane**.
- **Steam**: phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C and 60–70 atm → an **alcohol**.
- **Bromine**: room temperature, no catalyst → a **dibromo** compound, and the orange colour is **decolourised**.
- In a displayed formula, **every carbon has four bonds** and every bond is drawn as a line.

questions.prompt: Ethene reacts with hydrogen, with steam and with bromine. For each reaction, name or give the formula of the product, state the conditions needed, and explain what happens to the carbon–carbon double bond.
questions.solution: In all three reactions the atoms add across the carbon to carbon double bond, and the double bond becomes a single bond. With hydrogen, ethene forms ethane, C two H six, using a nickel catalyst at about one hundred and fifty degrees Celsius. With steam, ethene forms ethanol, C two H six O, using a phosphoric acid catalyst at about three hundred degrees Celsius and a pressure of sixty to seventy atmospheres. With bromine, ethene forms dibromoethane, C two H four Br two, and this happens at room temperature with no catalyst needed, which is why bromine water is decolourised by an alkene. In each case one atom or group joins each of the two carbon atoms, nothing else is formed, and the product is saturated.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The common pattern.** In all three, atoms add **across the C=C**, and the double bond becomes a **single** bond. Nothing else is formed, so all the atoms end up in one product, which is **saturated**.

**With hydrogen.**

$$C_2H_4 + H_2 \rightarrow C_2H_6$$

Ethane. Conditions: **nickel catalyst, about 150 °C**.

**With steam.**

$$C_2H_4 + H_2O \rightarrow C_2H_6O$$

Ethanol — an alcohol, because H goes to one carbon and OH to the other. Conditions: **phosphoric acid catalyst, about 300 °C, 60 to 70 atmospheres**.

**With bromine.**

$$C_2H_4 + Br_2 \rightarrow C_2H_4Br_2$$

Dibromoethane. Conditions: **room temperature, no catalyst**. Because it happens so readily, and because the orange Br₂ is used up, this is the test that **decolourises bromine water**.

The conditions carry marks of their own, so write them for each reaction rather than only naming the products.

questions.prompt: A student is given two colourless gases, one ethane and one ethene, and is asked to identify which is which. Describe a test they could use, state the result for each gas, and explain the result in terms of the bonding in the two molecules.
questions.solution: The student should bubble each gas separately through orange bromine water. The ethene will decolourise the bromine water, turning it from orange to colourless, while the ethane will leave it orange with no change. The reason is that ethene is unsaturated and contains a carbon to carbon double bond. Bromine adds across this double bond in an addition reaction, so the orange bromine molecules are used up and the colour disappears. Ethane is saturated and contains only single carbon to carbon bonds, so it has no double bond for the bromine to add across and no reaction takes place, leaving the colour unchanged.

questions.modelAnswer:
**The test.** Bubble each gas separately through **orange bromine water**.

**The results.**

- **Ethene**: the bromine water is **decolourised** — orange to colourless.
- **Ethane**: **no change**; it stays orange.

**The explanation.** Ethene is **unsaturated**: it has a **C=C double bond**. Bromine **adds across** that double bond in an addition reaction, so the orange Br₂ is used up and the colour goes.

Ethane is **saturated** — only single C–C bonds — so there is nothing for the bromine to add across, and no reaction happens.

Two points of wording that carry marks: say **decolourised**, not *turns clear*, because bromine water is already clear; and say the bromine is **used up**, which is what actually removes the colour.

examTechnique.body:
Say which family a molecule belongs to before doing anything else: the functional group decides the reaction.

For an addition reaction, write the alkene, write what is being added, and combine the atoms. Nothing else is formed, so the atoms must balance exactly.

Give the conditions with every reaction. They are separate marks from the product, and the three sets are easy to swap round.

In a displayed formula draw every bond as a line and give every carbon four bonds. Do not write CH3 in the corner of a displayed formula.

For the bromine water test, name the colour change in both directions — orange to colourless — and say the bromine is used up by addition across the double bond.

When explaining a smoky flame, name incomplete combustion and say that unburnt carbon leaves as soot.
examinerErrors: Writing CnH2n+2 for an alkene, which is the alkane formula.
Drawing a carbon with three or five bonds in a displayed formula.
Writing CH3 instead of drawing every C-H bond in a displayed formula.
Saying bromine water turns clear rather than colourless.
Swapping the nickel and phosphoric acid catalysts between the hydrogen and steam reactions.
Leaving out the temperature and pressure for the reaction with steam.
Writing a second product in an addition reaction, which only happens in substitution.
Saying an alkene burns cleanly, when the smoky flame is the point.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the C=C as the subject of the topic rather than a detail: it explains reactions by what happens at the double bond, not by recalling a list. It gives conditions alongside every product, because it knows those are separately marked. Its displayed formulae have four bonds at every carbon and every C–H drawn as a line. It says bromine water is decolourised and explains that addition uses the bromine up, rather than describing the colour change alone. And it can say why the same molecular formula, C4H8, can belong to more than one molecule.
